content: Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) is a live attenuated vaccine used to prevent tuberculosis and is typically administered intradermally at birth as part of the World Health Organization's global immunization program. While it is generally safe, it can cause adverse reactions, including localized, regional, distant, or disseminated complications, which may lead to significant distress for parents. In rare cases, BCG vaccination can result in severe illness or even death. The risk of complications is notably higher in children with immunocompromised conditions, such as those infected with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of various medical and surgical interventions for treating BCG-induced disease in children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, was conducted. Additional sources, such as conference proceedings and expert consultations, were also utilized. No language restrictions were applied during the search. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared different treatment modalities for BCG-induced disease in children. Two independent authors assessed the studies for inclusion and evaluated their risk of bias. The primary outcomes of interest were the failure rate of therapies for all types of BCG vaccine-induced complications and the time to resolution of illness, measured in months. Secondary outcomes included mortality due to BCG-induced disease and all-cause mortality. Risk ratios (RRs) were used to measure dichotomous outcomes, while mean differences were used for continuous outcomes. Five RCTs involving 341 children were included in the analysis. Four of these trials compared oral antibiotics to either no intervention or placebo. One trial evaluated needle aspiration versus no intervention, and another compared the use of locally instilled isoniazid to oral erythromycin. Two small studies assessed the efficacy of oral isoniazid, but the evidence was of very low quality, and it remains uncertain whether this intervention reduces clinical failure (RR 1.48; 95% CI 0.79 to 2.78; 54 participants). Similarly, the effect of oral erythromycin on clinical failure is uncertain (RR 1.03; 95% CI 0.70 to 1.53; 148 participants), as is the effect of oral isoniazid combined with rifampicin (RR 1.20; 95% CI 0.51 to 2.83; 35 participants). In cases of lymphadenitis abscess, needle aspiration may reduce the persistence of BCG-induced disease at 6 to 9 months of follow-up (RR 0.13; 95% CI 0.03 to 0.55; 77 participants, one study, low-quality evidence). Additionally, in another study involving patients with lymphadenitis abscess, aspiration combined with local instillation of isoniazid was found to reduce the time to clinical cure compared to aspiration combined with oral erythromycin (mean difference of 1.49 months less; 95% CI 0.82 to 2.15 less; 27 participants, one study). No RCTs specifically evaluated the use of antibiotics or other therapies for reducing clinical failure or time to resolution in HIV-infected infants with BCG-induced disease. Furthermore, no data were reported on mortality associated with interventions for treating BCG-induced disease. In conclusion, the effectiveness of oral antibiotics, including isoniazid, erythromycin, or a combination of isoniazid and rifampicin, for resolving BCG-induced disease remains unclear. Most cases of non-suppurative lymphadenitis resolve spontaneously within 4 to 6 months without treatment. However, patients with lymphadenitis abscess may benefit from needle aspiration, and local instillation of isoniazid could potentially shorten recovery time. The included studies were generally small and of low quality, highlighting the need for better-designed research. Future studies should focus on evaluating the use of needle aspiration and local instillation of isoniazid in cases of fluctuant lymph nodes. Additionally, therapeutic and preventive strategies for HIV-infected infants are crucial, given their higher risk of adverse outcomes.
